promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does xylem tissue transport in a plant?
options: Water and dissolved mineral ions
Sucrose and amino acids
Oxygen and carbon dioxide
Lipids and fatty acids
questions.explain: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots to the rest of the plant.

questions.q: Which substances are transported by phloem tissue?
options: Water and mineral ions only
Sucrose and amino acids
Carbon dioxide and oxygen
Starch and cellulose
questions.explain: Phloem transports manufactured substances such as sucrose and amino acids around the plant.

questions.q: Why are mature xylem vessels well adapted for transporting water?
options: They are hollow dead tubes with no cell contents to obstruct flow
They contain many mitochondria to pump water
They have thick living cytoplasm to hold water
They have cross walls that trap water
questions.explain: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes with lignified walls, allowing an uninterrupted column of water to move up the plant.

questions.q: In which direction does water move through the xylem?
options: Upwards, from roots to leaves
Downwards, from leaves to roots
In both directions equally
Only sideways between veins
questions.explain: Water moves in one direction through xylem: upwards from the roots to the leaves.

questions.q: What is the main function of a root hair cell?
options: To increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions
To carry out photosynthesis in the root
To store starch for the plant
To transport sucrose to the shoot
questions.explain: Root hair cells have a long thin extension that greatly increases surface area for the uptake of water and mineral ions.

questions.q: By which process does water enter a root hair cell from the soil?
options: Osmosis
Active transport
Respiration
Transpiration
questions.explain: Water moves into the root hair cell by osmosis, down a water potential gradient from the dilute soil solution.

questions.q: How are mineral ions such as nitrate ions taken up by root hair cells?
options: By active transport
By osmosis
By simple diffusion only
By evaporation
questions.explain: Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport, which requires energy and moves ions against their concentration gradient.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the pathway of water through a root?
options: Root hair cell to root cortex cells to xylem
Xylem to root hair cell to phloem
Phloem to cortex cells to root hair cell
Stomata to xylem to root hair cell
questions.explain: Water passes from the root hair cell across the cortex cells and into the xylem to be carried up the plant.

questions.q: What is transpiration?
options: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant
The uptake of mineral ions by the roots
The movement of sucrose in the phloem
The absorption of carbon dioxide by the leaves
questions.explain: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves, mainly by evaporation from mesophyll cells and diffusion out through the stomata.

questions.q: Through which structures is most water vapour lost from a leaf?
options: The stomata
The waxy cuticle
The xylem vessels
The root hairs
questions.explain: Most water vapour is lost by diffusion through the stomata, which are found mainly on the lower epidermis of the leaf.

questions.q: How does an increase in temperature affect the rate of transpiration?
options: It increases the rate of transpiration
It decreases the rate of transpiration
It has no effect on transpiration
It stops transpiration completely
questions.explain: Higher temperatures increase the rate of evaporation and diffusion of water vapour, raising the transpiration rate.

questions.q: Why does high humidity in the surrounding air reduce the rate of transpiration?
options: It reduces the water vapour concentration gradient between the leaf and the air
It closes the xylem vessels
It increases the wind speed around the leaf
It stops water entering the roots
questions.explain: High humidity means more water vapour outside the leaf, lowering the diffusion gradient so less water diffuses out.

questions.q: What effect does increased air movement (wind) have on transpiration?
options: It increases transpiration by removing water vapour from around the leaf
It decreases transpiration by adding water vapour to the leaf
It has no effect because stomata close in wind
It only affects water uptake by the roots
questions.explain: Wind carries away water vapour, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient and increasing the transpiration rate.

questions.q: A student uses a potometer and observes the air bubble move faster when a fan is switched on. What does this show?
options: Increased air movement increases the rate of water uptake and transpiration
Wind reduces the rate of transpiration
The plant has stopped transpiring
Water is now moving down the stem
questions.explain: A potometer estimates transpiration by measuring water uptake; faster bubble movement shows the fan has increased transpiration.

questions.q: What is translocation?
options: The movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem
The loss of water vapour from leaves
The uptake of water by osmosis in roots
The movement of water up the xylem
questions.explain: Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources to sinks.

questions.q: In translocation, what is meant by a 'source'?
options: A part of the plant that releases sucrose, such as a photosynthesising leaf
A part of the plant that stores or uses sucrose
The soil water absorbed by the roots
The stomata where water is lost
questions.explain: A source is a region that releases sucrose into the phloem, for example a leaf making sugars during photosynthesis.

questions.q: In summer sugars move from leaves to roots, but in spring sugars move from storage roots up to growing buds. What does this show about the phloem?
options: Phloem can transport substances in both directions depending on sources and sinks
Phloem only ever transports substances upwards
Phloem only ever transports substances downwards
Phloem transports only water
questions.explain: Unlike xylem, phloem can move assimilates in either direction, from whichever region is acting as the source to the sink.

questions.q: On a hot, dry, windy day a plant begins to wilt. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Transpiration is occurring faster than water can be taken up by the roots
The roots are absorbing too many mineral ions
Photosynthesis has stopped in the leaves
Sucrose is being translocated too quickly
questions.explain: When water loss by transpiration exceeds water uptake, cells lose turgor and the plant wilts.

questions.q: Two identical leafy shoots are set up: shoot A in still, humid air and shoot B in dry, moving air. Which shoot transpires faster and why?
options: Shoot B, because dry moving air increases the diffusion gradient for water vapour
Shoot A, because humid air speeds up evaporation
Both transpire at exactly the same rate
Shoot A, because still air removes water vapour faster
questions.explain: Dry, moving air keeps the water vapour concentration outside the leaf low, maintaining a steep gradient and faster transpiration.

questions.q: In the vascular bundle of a dicotyledonous leaf, where is the xylem usually located relative to the phloem?
options: Towards the upper surface, above the phloem
Towards the lower surface, below the phloem
Surrounding the phloem on all sides
Only in the epidermis of the leaf
questions.explain: In a leaf vein the xylem lies on the upper side of the vascular bundle and the phloem on the lower side.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610) syllabus; Transport in Plants
